newsitem.title: USA: Hartford chief sees better ROE ahead.
newsitem.headline: Hartford chief sees better ROE ahead.

text.p: Diversified insurer The Hartford thinks it has taken the right steps to improve its annual return on equity (ROE) to the 13 to 15 percent range, its chairman and chief executive Ramani Ayer said on Monday.
"We have strengthened our balance sheet, eliminated our drags, and we are excited about where we're going," Ayer told Reuters in an interview.

The Hartford released its fourth quarter results earlier on Monday. ROE for the full year was 12.5 percent. "We are continuing to move in the direction of 13 to 15 percent ROE as a company," said Ayer.
Ayer said the company eliminated a big earnings drag by taking a $510 million environmental and asbestos charge in the third quarter of 1996.

Ayer, who took over as chairman and chief executive two days ago after Don Frahm retired, said The Hartford wanted to become a major global player in five core areas: life, commercial property-casualty, personal lines property-casualty, reinsurance, and international business.
"We want to be global," he said. "We continue to push to achieve leadership positions in all of these businesses -- that's very much the nature of our strategy."
The company intends to sniff out acquisition opportunities both in the U.S. and overseas, said Ayer.

"Our strategy has been in the direction of creating focussed acquisitions," he said. "We continue to believe that there are opportunities on a focussed basis, both nationally and internationally," he said, but did not elaborate.
Ayer said the American Association of Retired Persons (AARP) segment of The Hartford's personal lines business had solid growth potential.
"AARP continues to be a good growth story. We're fairly competitive... so I'm excited about where AARP is going and we'll continue to grow as a business in AARP."

Ayer said that in addition to eliminating the company's historical earnings drag, "We think our capital position has strengthened, we think our businesses are doing well, and there's good growth opportunity as we look ahead."
Ayer would not comment on projected earnings for 1997.
Analyst Pete Wade of Lehman Bros told Reuters he estimated The Hartford's 1997 earnings at $6.40 per share.
He said he had not decided whether to raise his forecast based on Monday's slightly higher than expected results.
